title: Linux Foundation KCNA
summary: The Kubernetes and Cloud Native Associate, exam code KCNA, is an entry level certification from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, which is hosted by the Linux Foundation. It is aimed at people who are starting to work with containers and Kubernetes and who want a formal, vendor neutral first step before a deeper administrator exam. The level is associate, so the paper tests broad understanding of the ecosystem rather than deep cluster surgery. Passing it tells an employer that you know how containers are orchestrated, how cloud native applications are built and delivered, and how such systems are observed. The exam is delivered online and is proctored, and it consists of multiple choice questions rather than a hands on lab. It supports roles such as junior DevOps engineer, site reliability engineer, platform support engineer and cloud native developer. The domain structure below follows the published objectives, so check the current version with the Linux Foundation before booking. This is an independent study guide and is not endorsed by the Linux Foundation or the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.

beginner.definition: This is an entry level certificate from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. It covers Kubernetes and cloud native technology. Kubernetes is a tool that runs application containers across many computers and keeps them healthy. The associate level means the exam checks ideas more than repairs to a live cluster.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most modern software is packaged in containers and run on Kubernetes. Teams need people who understand that world. They also need people who are not yet the cluster expert. This certificate shows an employer that you speak the language of containers and orchestration. It is also a sensible first step before a harder administrator exam, and it fits career changers and junior engineers.
howItWorks: Learn what a container is and how it differs from a virtual machine, then run one on your own laptop.
Study the main Kubernetes objects, such as pod, deployment, service and namespace, and what each one does.
Read about cloud native architecture, including microservices, serverless functions and the role of an application programming interface.
Learn how code reaches production, including continuous integration, continuous delivery and Git based workflows.
Study observability, which means logs, metrics and traces, and why a running system must be watched.
Take practice questions until you can explain each answer, then sit the online proctored exam.
beginner.example: Think of a large hotel. Each guest room is like a container, because it holds one guest in an isolated space. The reception desk is like Kubernetes, because it decides which room each guest receives. It also moves a guest if a floor is closed. The hotel manager watches the electricity, the water and the complaints, which is observability. A KCNA candidate understands how those three parts work together, even before taking charge of the building.
takeaways: You can pass this exam without running a large cluster, but hands on practice makes the ideas stay.
Learn the vocabulary of cloud native work, because interviews use the same words as the exam.
Always confirm the current objectives and domain weights on the Linux Foundation website before booking.

objectives: Explain what Kubernetes is and how it differs from running containers by hand
Describe the main Kubernetes objects and the job each one performs
Explain container orchestration concerns such as scheduling, scaling and self healing
Describe how cloud native applications are packaged, delivered and released
Explain observability, including logs, metrics and traces, and why it matters in production
Identify the wider cloud native ecosystem, including the projects around Kubernetes

chapters.title: Kubernetes fundamentals
objectives: Explain what Kubernetes does and which problem it solves for teams that run many containers
Describe the control plane and the worker node, and what each component is responsible for
Explain what a pod is and how containers inside one pod share storage and network
Use controllers such as deployments and replica sets to keep a declared number of copies running
Expose an application inside and outside the cluster with services and ingress rules
Separate workloads with namespaces and store configuration and secrets away from the image
Read and interpret a Kubernetes manifest written in YAML, the plain text configuration format

chapters.title: Container orchestration
objectives: Explain how the scheduler chooses a node for each workload and what limits that choice
Describe how the cluster reacts when a pod or a node fails and how the workload is restored
Explain horizontal and vertical scaling and choose the right approach for a workload
Compare container runtimes and explain the role of the container network and storage interfaces
Describe how stateful workloads differ from stateless ones in an orchestrated environment

chapters.title: Cloud native application delivery
objectives: Describe the software delivery lifecycle from code commit to a running release
Explain continuous integration and continuous delivery and how they reduce release risk
Explain Git based workflows and the role of declarative configuration in deployment
Describe how an application is packaged as an image and how images are stored and versioned
Explain how a rollout is paused or reversed when a new version behaves badly

chapters.title: Cloud native architecture
objectives: Compare monolithic and microservice designs and state the trade-offs of each
Explain how serverless functions and managed services fit into a cloud native design
Describe the role of application programming interfaces and service to service communication
Explain how cloud native principles such as automation and portability shape design decisions
Describe how observability and telemetry are designed into an application rather than added later
Explain the purpose of the wider cloud native project ecosystem around Kubernetes
